Intervention Geometry — Confirmatory Study

V-JEPA 2 embedding response to one-factor physics interventions on a simulated falling/bouncing sphere

This is the confirmatory study, at design-doc scale. 1200 base worlds, 10797 accepted clips, GPU-rendered with Blender EEVEE on the fully validated v4 pipeline (correct camera, physics, and lighting — see the methods report for the calibration history). This run also survived a real mid-run infrastructure interruption: the GPU pod crashed partway through with ~88% of clips already encoded; the persistent volume's data was verified byte-for-byte intact (manifest checksum match), and the remaining clips were regenerated and encoded to finish the exact same deterministic dataset — every one of the 10797 clips below is accounted for, none silently dropped or duplicated. Model: facebook/vjepa2-vitl-fpc64-256, a documented substitution for the docx's unpublished ViT-B/16 384px checkpoint.

Base world: one random starting position/velocity for the sphere, simulated once per physics setting (baseline plus each intervention), so every version of a world starts identically and only the one changed constant differs. Accepted clips: 10,797 of 10,800 rendered clips (1,200 worlds × 9 versions) passed the visibility check described below — only 3 rejected, a 0.03% rate. Feature dim = 32,768: explained in the next card. Rank used = 8: this matches the docx's confirmatory-design rank exactly — at this scale there's no need to cap it down the way the 25-world engineering pilot had to (rank 3). Weights hash: a real fingerprint of the exact V-JEPA weights used for every clip in this run, confirmed identical across the pre-crash and post-recovery encoding passes.

How a video becomes one number: Δz

What Δz is

Every chart below is built from one quantity: for a given base world and a given physical factor (say, gravity), we render two clips that are identical in every way — same start position, same start velocity, same random seed — except that one constant (gravity) is set to a different value. We run both clips through the frozen V-JEPA encoder to get two vectors, then subtract:

Δz = z(intervention clip) − z(baseline clip)

Δz is a list of 32,768 numbers describing exactly how the model's internal representation moved, purely because of that one changed physical constant and nothing else.

How each z (32,768 numbers) is built
  1. Take 64 frames evenly spaced across the 6-second clip (the model's required input length).
  2. Run them through the frozen encoder. Its output is 8,192 "tokens" × 1,024 numbers each.
  3. Those 8,192 tokens are really 32 time-steps × 256 spatial patches (16×16 grid over the 256×256 frame), each a 1,024-number vector — confirmed from the model's own patch-embedding code, which lays tokens out in that time-major order.
  4. Average the 256 spatial patches together at each of the 32 time-steps, leaving 32 vectors of 1,024 numbers.
  5. Lay those 32 vectors end to end: 32 × 1,024 = 32,768 numbers. That is z.

This matches the design doc's rule: keep the model's own time resolution instead of averaging the whole clip into one blurred snapshot.

Two real rendered clips from world000 (actual video, not a static frame strip) — the same Blender-EEVEE, v4-camera pipeline that produced every clip this page's numbers are computed from. These two use a camera that tracks (crops around) the sphere purely so it reads clearly at dashboard size; the fixed, non-tracking camera in sim/render.py is what actually encodes into V-JEPA and is what the camera-projection math in the companion methods report describes.

Uncentered SVD spectrum

What it measures

For one factor (e.g. gravity), stack every Δz we have for it into a table: one row per world/intervention pair, 32,768 columns. Singular value decomposition (SVD) finds a set of directions, ranked by how much of the rows' total squared length ("energy") each one accounts for.

How the chart is computed
cumulative energy at rank r = (sum of top-r singular values²) / (sum of all singular values²)

r90 = the smallest r where that fraction reaches 90%. A truly compact code would keep r90 small and flat no matter how many worlds you add.

What the result actually shows here

With 2,400 Δz pairs per factor (2,397 for velocity), r90 is nowhere near the sample count anymore — this is a real read on compactness, not a small-sample artifact. r90 ranges from 46 (restitution) to 142 (friction) out of 2,400: restitution's effect is the most concentrated (90% of its energy in under 2% of the available directions), while friction's is the most spread out (90% needs nearly 6%). That ordering is the opposite of what the 25-world pilot suggested, where friction looked most compact — at pilot scale, r90 for a near-zero effect (see friction's mean-shift fraction below) mostly reflected noise structure in too few samples, not a real property of the signal. None of the four factors are extremely low-rank in the docx's strictest sense (r90 ≫ 8), but all sit far below full rank (2,400), consistent with a structured, if not maximally compact, code.

Specificity matrix

What it measures

Fit a rank-8 basis using only one factor's Δz vectors (the row). Project a different factor's Δz vectors (the column) onto that basis and measure what fraction of their energy it recovers:

retention = 1 − ‖residual‖² / ‖original‖²

If gravity's own basis explains gravity's changes much better than friction's basis does, that's evidence gravity has its own distinct direction rather than all factors just producing generic "the ball moved differently" motion.

A fix worth knowing about

An earlier version of this matrix fit and tested the diagonal on the same data, which trivially made every diagonal cell look better than the off-diagonal cells regardless of any real signal. The diagonal here uses the same held-out (leave-one-world-out) retention as the chart below, so every cell — diagonal included — is tested on data its basis never saw.

What the result actually shows here

Gravity, restitution, and velocity are each specific: each factor's own diagonal cell is the largest value in its row (gravity 0.667, restitution 0.727, velocity 0.485), meaning each factor's basis reconstructs its own held-out effect far better than any other factor's basis does. All three retention values are higher than the 25-world pilot found (0.638, 0.678, 0.391) — the pattern didn't just survive 48× more data, it got stronger, which is what a real effect should do as sample size grows. Gravity and restitution show real cross-talk with each other (gravity's basis retains 0.331 of restitution's effect, restitution's retains 0.277 of gravity's) — physically sensible, since both act on the sphere's vertical dynamics. Friction still shows no specificity: its own diagonal (0.096) is not the largest value in its row — velocity's basis (0.131) explains friction's held-out variation better than friction's own basis does. Friction's mean-shift energy fraction (visible below) is essentially zero at this scale, reinforcing that V-JEPA's embedding barely registers this friction range as a distinct signal, rather than registering it as a signal that gets confused with other factors.

Leave-one-world-out rank retention

What it measures

Whether a direction learned from some worlds actually predicts the direction of change in a new world it never saw — the generalization test every number above depends on.

How it's computed
  1. Hold out one world's Δz vectors for this factor.
  2. Fit a rank-8 uncentered SVD basis on the remaining worlds' Δz vectors only.
  3. Project the held-out world's Δz onto that basis and measure retained energy (same formula as the specificity matrix).
  4. Repeat once per world (1,200 folds here), average the 1,200 retention values.
A number to calibrate against

A random rank-8 direction in a 32,768-dimensional space would be expected to explain about rank / dimension = 8 / 32,768 ≈ 0.00024 of a held-out vector's energy purely by chance (the math memo's H₀-geometry null). Every bar below (0.096–0.727) sits far above that chance floor. Gravity, restitution, and velocity all clear 0.48–0.73 — a strong, structured signal, not noise, now measured across 1,200 held-out folds instead of 25. Friction sits at 0.096: well above the chance floor, so the model is not completely blind to friction, but well below the other three factors and (per the specificity matrix) still not even the best-explaining basis for its own effect.

Fit rank-8 basis on all-but-one world, measure retained energy on the held-out world's Δz. Dots are individual folds (n=1200).

Per-factor summary

Mean-shift energy fraction, explained

What share of a factor's average Δz-squared-length is explained just by one single "always shift this way" vector (the mean of all its Δz), versus needing a different direction per world:

fraction = ‖mean(Δz)‖² / mean(‖Δz‖²)

Low across the board except restitution — every factor's effect direction depends noticeably on the specific world rather than being one constant shift added to every embedding. Restitution is by far the highest (20%): changing bounciness produces the most world-independent, consistent embedding shift of the four. Friction is essentially zero (0.05%) — consistent with everything else on this page, its effect doesn't even have a consistent average direction, let alone a specific one.
